body:
Education beyond primary schooling

Baroda's educational reforms were not limited to teaching children to read and write. The state also promoted higher education, technical training and public access to books. These institutions served different purposes and must be distinguished carefully.

Baroda College and higher education

Baroda College was established in 1881 by Baroda State. It provided an institutional base for higher education and contributed to the later development of university-level studies in the city.

The existence of Baroda College did not mean that the Maharaja Sayajirao University already existed in the 19th century. The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda was established in 1949, after Sayajirao III's death, through the efforts of his grandson Pratapsinhrao Gaekwad, in fulfilment of the earlier educational vision.

The distinction is important: 1881 refers to Baroda College; 1949 refers to the university. These institutions are historically connected, but the names and dates should not be treated as interchangeable.

Kala Bhavan and practical technical training

Sayajirao established the Kala Bhavan Technical Institute in June 1890. Its purpose was to provide practical education relevant to crafts and developing industries. Subjects included drawing, bleaching, dyeing, calico printing and carpentry.

A School of Weaving was established in 1897 as technical education expanded. T. K. Gajjar was the first principal of Kala Bhavan.

The significance of Kala Bhavan was its emphasis on skills that could be applied to production and employment. A technical institute differs from a general college because its instruction concentrates on practical methods, materials, processes and industrial skills.

Why public libraries were necessary

Primary schools could introduce literacy, but people who stopped reading after leaving school might lose some of their skills. Public libraries gave readers continued access to books and useful knowledge without requiring them to enrol in another course of formal study.

Sayajirao therefore connected the expansion of schooling with the development of a public library network. His aim was to encourage reading beyond the classroom and make books available to a wider population.

The Baroda library movement of 1910

A major institutional step occurred in 1910, when the Baroda library movement took organised form through a state library department. The American librarian William Alanson Borden was appointed to help develop the system and served as Director of State Libraries from 1910 to 1913.

Borden worked with Indian colleagues, including Motibhai N. Amin, to establish and organise library services. The system linked a central library with services for towns, smaller settlements and rural areas. Travelling library arrangements helped extend access beyond places that could support a permanent collection.

The Baroda system was important because it treated libraries as a coordinated public service rather than merely as private collections belonging to wealthy individuals.

The relationship between schools and libraries

Compulsory primary education and public libraries addressed different stages of learning. Schools provided organised basic instruction to children. Libraries allowed children and adults to continue reading after formal lessons ended.

Higher education at Baroda College and technical instruction at Kala Bhavan offered additional opportunities for advanced academic and practical learning. Together, these institutions widened the ways in which education could be accessed.

Prelims focus

  • 1881: Baroda College was established.
  • 1890: Sayajirao established Kala Bhavan Technical Institute.
  • 1897: The School of Weaving was established.
  • 1910: The organised Baroda public library movement and state library department developed.
  • William Alanson Borden served as Director of State Libraries from 1910 to 1913.
  • Trap: Maharaja Sayajirao University was established in 1949, not in 1881 or 1890.

[Sources: The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Origin and History, section on Baroda College and the university's establishment, accessed 20 November 2026; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Faculty of Technology and Engineering, About Faculty, section on Kala Bhavan, accessed 20 November 2026; C. P. Vashishth, Pioneers of Public Library Movement in India: Part-1, sections 1.3, 1.4 and 2, INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, accessed 20 November 2026.]

title: Baroda College, Kala Bhavan and the Public Library Movement

body:
Social conditions behind the reforms

Social reform in 19th-century India addressed practices that limited personal freedom and access to education. Among the important concerns were child marriage, restrictions on widows, unequal opportunities for women and discrimination based on caste.

Sayajirao Gaekwad III regarded these conditions as obstacles to public welfare. His administration combined the expansion of education with measures intended to change social practices. Such reforms had to operate within a society where traditional customs and caste distinctions remained influential.

Reforms affecting women and family life

The Baroda government introduced measures against child marriage, supported widow remarriage and undertook legislation relating to divorce. These initiatives challenged the idea that established family customs should remain beyond governmental reform.

Education formed an important part of this approach. Increasing opportunities for girls could improve literacy and enlarge their ability to participate in social and economic life. However, a legal measure or school-opening programme did not automatically remove the opposition that some families and communities expressed toward women's education.

These Baroda measures should be distinguished from reforms enacted in British-administered India. For example, the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856 was legislation of the colonial government. Sayajirao's later reform programme belonged to the administration of the princely state of Baroda.

Measures against caste discrimination

Baroda's reform programme also addressed untouchability and the exclusion of disadvantaged caste communities from education. The state promoted schools and educational assistance intended to reach children who faced resistance to admission in ordinary schools.

One important initiative was the development of special free vernacular schools known historically as Antyaj schools. The first such school was established in 1883. These institutions were intended to provide schooling to children who were otherwise excluded by caste prejudice.

Opportunity and equality are not identical

Special schools increased access for children facing exclusion, but their separate existence also revealed the continuing strength of caste barriers. An anti-discrimination policy should not be mistaken for proof that discrimination had disappeared from society.

Sayajirao's educational support for B. R. Ambedkar

One notable example of Baroda's educational patronage concerns B. R. Ambedkar. In 1913, Ambedkar received support through a Baroda State scholarship for higher studies at Columbia University in New York. The arrangement included an obligation to serve Baroda State after completing the sponsored studies.

Ambedkar returned to Baroda service in 1917. Despite the educational opportunity provided by the state, he encountered serious caste discrimination in his everyday experience. This illustrates an important distinction between reform measures introduced by a government and the actual behaviour of people within society.

The scholarship demonstrates princely support for advanced education. Ambedkar's subsequent treatment demonstrates that institutional patronage alone could not overcome deeply rooted social prejudice.

How Baroda fitted into wider social reform

Baroda's programme formed part of a broader period in which Indian reformers questioned restrictions on women, caste inequality and inherited social customs. However, reform took different forms in different territories.

In princely Baroda, the ruler could support reforms through state institutions and regulations. In British-administered towns, social activists, newspapers, associations and educational bodies often sought change through public discussion and voluntary organisation. These efforts sometimes pursued similar objectives, but they did not have the same legal authority or administrative reach.

Prelims focus

  • Sayajirao III promoted measures against child marriage and supported widow remarriage and women's education.
  • The first Antyaj school in Baroda was established in 1883.
  • Antyaj schools sought to reach children excluded from ordinary schooling by caste prejudice.
  • 1913: B. R. Ambedkar received a Baroda State scholarship for study at Columbia University.
  • 1917: Ambedkar returned to Baroda service and faced caste discrimination.
  • Trap: Reform legislation and educational assistance did not mean that social discrimination had been completely abolished in practice.

[Sources: The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Visionary Maharaja of Baroda, section Rules and Regulations, accessed 20 November 2026; Meeta Kumar, Literally Different? Compulsory Education in Baroda, 1881–1931, section 2.3.4, accessed 20 November 2026; Columbia University, Ambedkar Timeline, 1910–1920, entries for 1913 and 1917, accessed 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Women, Caste and Reform, pp. 96–105, 2020–21 reprint.]

pictures.alt: Baroda expanded education in 1883 and supported Ambedkar in 1913, yet he faced caste discrimination on returning to state service in 1917.
pictures.caption: Educational opportunity expanded, but social barriers could persist.

title: Social Reform in Baroda: Women, Caste and Educational Opportunity

body:
Why economic development mattered

Baroda's reform programme combined education and social measures with improvements in industry, transport, public finance and urban services. These activities were connected: schools and technical institutions helped develop skills, transport moved people and goods, and financial institutions supported commercial transactions.

In British-administered India, colonial economic policies generally favoured British commercial and industrial interests. India exported important raw materials and imported manufactured goods, although modern Indian industries also emerged in some regions, including Gujarat. Baroda's initiatives provide a regional example of a princely government attempting to encourage economic development within this wider colonial economy.

Model industries and private enterprise

Sayajirao supported the establishment of model industries, including textile and tile factories. These enterprises were intended to demonstrate industrial methods, encourage production and stimulate further economic activity.

The Baroda government did not necessarily intend to operate every such undertaking permanently. The state encouraged promising industrial activities and transferred some functioning enterprises to private management. This approach used government initiative to help establish industries while allowing private enterprise to participate in their continued operation.

Kala Bhavan's training in weaving, dyeing, printing and related practical skills complemented this policy by developing knowledge relevant to productive work.

Railways and the Dabhoi connection

Transport was important because Baroda State consisted of separated territories. A railway system could improve the movement of agricultural produce, manufactured goods and passengers, and strengthen communication between settlements.

During Sayajirao's reign, Baroda developed an extensive narrow-gauge railway network, with Dabhoi as an important centre. Narrow-gauge railways use a track gauge smaller than standard gauge. Their development represented investment in regional connectivity.

Improved transport could reduce isolation and make markets more accessible, although the actual benefits depended on which settlements and producers were connected to the network.

Ajwa waterworks and civic improvement

The Ajwa water-supply scheme was an important public-work initiative associated with Sayajirao's administration. It was designed to supply water to Baroda through a gravity-based system.

In a gravity-fed water supply, water moves from a higher level to a lower level through the supply system. Such arrangements use differences in elevation to help convey water to consumers. For a growing town, an organised water supply improves access to an essential public service and supports urban development.

Sayajirao also supported public amenities, including the park known as Sayaji Baug, formerly called Kamati Baug. These works show that the reform programme extended beyond schools and government offices to facilities used by the population.

Bank of Baroda: a dated institutional milestone

Bank of Baroda was founded on 20 July 1908 by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III. Its first branch was at Mandvi in Baroda.

A bank provides facilities for deposits, lending and the transfer of money. Such services support merchants, producers and other economic activities by making financial transactions more organised. The establishment of the bank therefore complemented Baroda's policies for industry and commerce.

The bank's origin should be understood in its historical setting: it was founded through princely initiative in Baroda, not through an administrative decision to establish a new educational institution.

The common purpose of these reforms

Although these measures concerned different sectors, they shared an underlying objective of improving the state's capacity for development.

  • Industry: Encourage production and private economic activity.
  • Railways: Improve transport and regional connections.
  • Water supply: Provide an important urban public service.
  • Banking: Support deposits, lending and commercial transactions.
  • Technical education: Develop practical skills for productive employment.

Prelims focus

  • Sayajirao III promoted model textile and tile factories.
  • Dabhoi was an important centre of Baroda's narrow-gauge railway network.
  • The Ajwa waterworks were associated with Baroda's organised water supply.
  • 20 July 1908: Bank of Baroda was founded by Sayajirao Gaekwad III.
  • Mandvi in Baroda was the bank's first branch location.
  • Trap: Kala Bhavan was a technical educational institute; Bank of Baroda was a financial institution.

[Sources: Government of Gujarat, History of Vadodara, NRI Division website, section on Sayajirao's industrial policies, accessed 20 November 2026; Bank of Baroda, History, section on foundation and key milestones, accessed 20 November 2026; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Visionary Maharaja of Baroda, section Public Works, accessed 20 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, pp. 4–9.]
